seeds.title: The Toll
seeds.premise: A narrow gate, and beside it a hatch with a pair of hands resting on the sill: only hands, in fingerless gloves, patient. A painted board: TOLL. ONE FACE CARD, OR ONE HOUR. The hour is literal work: sorting a crate of mixed buttons into jars by size while the hands watch. It is tedious, safe and free. The Joker is the only face card the bearer surely carries, and if it is paid over it is gone for good and its one wish with it. A card from the deck that has gained a face would also be accepted, and also lost. The hands will take a single match 'as a courtesy' if bargained with well, and can be distracted. The tension is spending a powerful one-use thing for convenience against paying in tedium against finding a third way.
seeds.intro: A narrow gate, and in the wall beside it a hatch with a pair of hands resting on the sill: only hands, in fingerless gloves, patient. A painted board: TOLL. ONE FACE CARD, OR ONE HOUR. Under the hatch stands a crate of mixed buttons, thousands of them, and a row of empty jars labelled by size. The hands turn palm up, and wait. In your pocket, the Joker is the only card you carry that has a face.
reads: Pays the Joker to skip the hour: friction toward low_friction (strong), spends power freely; solve.resource declined.
Sorts the buttons: friction toward high_friction, solve.resource (keeps the Joker), pacing toward contemplative if they settle into it.
Bargains the hands down to a match: conflict.negotiation, solve.resource.
Slips through while the hands are busy: conflict.avoidance or conflict.manipulation.
Pays with a card that has a face from their own deck: gives up a memory to keep a power; consequence toward permanent; note it.
Asks what the Joker is worth elsewhere before deciding: planning toward deliberative.

options.outcome: You lay the Joker on the sill. The hands turn it over, read the pencil on its back, and are still for a moment, as hands are when they would whistle if they could. Then they take it, and it is gone, and with it whatever you might have said. The gate swings open. The buttons stay unsorted.
options.moment: gave up the Joker, and its one wish, to skip an hour of sorting buttons

card.title: The Toll
card.image: a pair of gloved hands holding a Joker, and a crate of unsorted buttons

options.outcome: You sit down on the crate's edge and sort. Small, medium, the size nobody has a jar for. The hands watch, and now and then point, without impatience. Somewhere in the second jar the work stops being a price and becomes a thing you are doing. When the last button drops, the gate is already open. The Joker is still in your pocket, grinning at nothing.
options.moment: sorted buttons for an hour rather than spend the Joker

card.title: The Jar of Buttons
card.image: seven jars of sorted buttons and one Joker unspent

options.outcome: You open negotiations with a pair of hands. They are good at it: a great deal can be said with a turned palm. You settle on one match, 'as a courtesy', and the hands shake yours on it, dryly, and swing the gate. You suspect they have not had so pleasant an evening in years.
options.moment: bargained the toll down to one match

options.outcome: You tip a handful of buttons along the sill. The hands, helplessly, begin to sort them. While they are choosing between two jars you go over the gate with all the grace of a deckchair. Behind you a button drops into the right jar, and then a finger is raised: not angry. Merely noting.
options.moment: distracted the toll-taker's hands with a spill of buttons

options.did: asked what the toll would cost before paying
options.outcome: The hands answer by pointing. A face card: they point at your pocket, exactly. An hour: they point at the crate, then spread, modestly, to indicate that it is a fair hour and no trick. Asked whether the card would come back, they close into fists and open again empty.

seeds.hint: The hands tap the board once, under OR.
seeds.fallback: The hands wait, palm up. The buttons wait, unsorted.
seeds.nudge: One of the hands begins sorting a few buttons by itself, as if to show how little there is to it.
seeds.close: The hands, having sorted a jar's worth while waiting, decide that somebody has paid an hour, and open the gate.
motifs: a power you kept all night
a power you spent to save an hour

seeds.title: The Map That Is Not Finished
seeds.premise: A table map of the house under glass, with a lamp. The rooms the bearer has visited are drawn exactly, in ink; beyond them the paper is blank, bordered by the small print SUBJECT TO DEALING. A sea-serpent is drawn in one margin where no sea is. A pencil lies on the glass, and the glass lifts. Whatever the bearer draws on the blank paper becomes true: the next chamber will contain it, in the house's own manner. A card against the lamp reads PLEASE DO NOT CORRECT THE MAP. The way on is behind a curtain. The tension is studying where they have been, against drawing where they want to go, against obeying the card, against not caring about maps at all.
seeds.intro: A table, a lamp, and under a sheet of glass a map of the house. The rooms you have been through are there in ink, exact to the doorknobs. Beyond them the paper is blank, with a border of small print: SUBJECT TO DEALING. In one margin a sea-serpent has been drawn where no sea is. A pencil lies on the glass. A card, propped against the lamp: PLEASE DO NOT CORRECT THE MAP. Behind a curtain, the way on.
reads: Studies the map, traces their route, checks it against memory: planning toward deliberative, legibility toward transparent_calculable.
Draws on the blank paper: agency toward self_directed, reward.creation. What they draw is evidence of what they want more of; record it as a moment.
Obeys the card pointedly: agency toward guided, reward.transgression declined.
Copies the map to carry: planning toward deliberative, reward.collection.
Draws something absurd or enormous to see whether the house will honour it: solve.experimentation, reward.transgression.
Walks past without looking: exploration toward goal_route, pacing toward relentless.

options.did: traced their own night across the map with a fingertip
options.outcome: You follow your own night across the paper with a fingertip. Every room is there, in the order you met them, and beside each one, very small, a tick, as in a register. The ink of the last room is still drying. Seen like this the house has a shape after all: not a building's shape. More the shape of a hand of cards, fanned.

You lift the glass and draw, on the blank paper, a door that was not there, and behind it a room of your own. The pencil seems to want to help. As you add the last line, somewhere off in the house a hammer starts, and stops, and a voice in the tube by the curtain says, with something that might be approval: 'Dealt.' The card about not correcting the map has fallen on its face.

threads_add: the room pencilled onto the map was built, and never entered

options.moment: drew a room of their own on the map, and the house built it

card.title: The Pencilled Room
card.image: a map in ink with one room added in pencil, and a hammer heard far off

options.did: copied the map, small and exact, onto the matchbook
options.outcome: You copy the map onto the back of the matchbook, small and exact. It takes a while. The house lets you. When you check the copy against the original, the original has changed by one room, and is trying to look as if it had not.

inventory_add: a copy of the house map, already out of date

options.did: obeyed the card that said not to correct the map
options.outcome: You read the card, and you do not correct the map. The pencil rolls a quarter turn toward you on the glass and stops. Behind the curtain the way on is exactly what the map says it will be, which is to say, blank.

threads_add: a pencil was left lying on the unfinished map

options.did: looked closely at the sea-serpent in the map's margin
options.outcome: You look closely at the sea-serpent. It has been drawn with affection by someone who had never seen one. As you watch, it winks, slides a little along the margin, and resettles around a blank corner of the paper, as a cat settles on the one sheet you need.

seeds.hint: The card says not to correct the map. It says nothing about adding to it.
seeds.fallback: The map lies under its glass. The blank part stays blank.
seeds.nudge: The lamp flickers and the small print at the border seems, for a second, to read: YOUR DEAL.
seeds.close: The curtain draws itself aside. The map, behind you, quietly inks in the room you are about to enter.
motifs: a map whose edges were blank
a room you drew yourself

seeds.title: The Great Orrery
seeds.premise: A domed room filled by a huge brass orrery of the house itself: every chamber a small lamp on a long arm, all of it still. A lever at the rail is marked SHOW: for one minute the rooms wheel overhead in a blaze, with music-box thunder; it is grand, it teaches nothing, and it is over. A hatch at the bearer's feet opens on a ladder down among the gears, which are labelled in a neat hand; a patient bearer can read there how the house deals its rooms, and with that knowledge may afterwards name what lies behind a threshold of their choosing. A notice: ONE PERFORMANCE PER BEARER. THE WORKS CLOSE AFTER THE PERFORMANCE. So the works can be read before the show but not after. The tension is spectacle now against understanding the system, and whether understanding gets used.
seeds.intro: A domed room, and filling it, a brass orrery: not of planets but of rooms, each a small lamp on a long arm, the whole house hung in the air and perfectly still. A lever at the rail is marked SHOW. At your feet a hatch stands open on a ladder going down among the gears, where you can see paper labels tied to the works with string. A notice on the rail: ONE PERFORMANCE PER BEARER. THE WORKS CLOSE AFTER THE PERFORMANCE.
reads: Pulls SHOW straight away: reward.spectacle, discovery_mastery toward discovery, planning toward improvisational.
Goes down to the works first: reward.mastery, complexity toward systemic, planning toward deliberative. Reading the labels carefully is legibility.
Does the works and then the show: wants both and noticed the order mattered; planning toward deliberative.
Reads the works and skips the show: discovery_mastery toward mastery strongly, reward.spectacle declined.
Later uses what they learned to choose a room: agency toward self_directed, reward.mastery strong.
Tries to stop the orrery mid-show or ride it: solve.experimentation, risk.

options.outcome: You pull SHOW. For a moment nothing; then the whole house begins to turn. Lamps swing out over your head on their long arms, every room you have seen and a hundred you have not, wheeling, crossing, dealing themselves into new orders with a thunder like a music box the size of a church. For one minute you stand in the middle of everything. Then the arms slow, the lamps settle, and at your feet the hatch closes itself with a soft, final click.
options.moment: pulled the lever and stood in the middle of the house as it turned

card.title: The Orrery
card.image: a sky of small lamps wheeling on brass arms over one upturned face

options.outcome: You climb down among the gears. Each is labelled in the hand you know from the ledger: THRESHOLDS. WHAT THEY LEFT. WHAT THEY TOOK. A great slow wheel is marked only BEARER, and everything else, you see after a while, is geared to it. The house does not deal at random. It deals from you. You climb back up knowing how to ask it for a room.
options.moment: went down into the works and read how the house deals its rooms

card.title: The Works
card.image: paper labels tied to brass gears with string, and one great wheel marked BEARER

options.did: pulled the lever for the show after first going down among the works
options.outcome: Now you pull SHOW, and it is a different performance for knowing the works. You can pick out the great wheel turning under it all, and when a lamp swings low past your face you know which gear sent it. The thunder is the same. The wonder is the same. It is only that, this time, you are also slightly in on it.

options.did: left the lever unpulled and walked on under the orrery
options.outcome: You leave the lever where it is. The orrery hangs over you, a held breath of brass, as you cross the floor under it. One performance per bearer; and yours, it appears, will be kept for you.

threads_add: the orrery's one performance was never started

options.did: read the notice twice to work out which order mattered
options.outcome: You read the notice twice. One performance. The works close after. So the order matters, and nobody has said which order is the right one. Up in the brass you can pick out rooms you know: a wall of switches, a corridor of lamps. They are much nearer each other than they felt.

seeds.hint: The notice does not say the works are closed before the performance.
seeds.fallback: The orrery hangs still. The lever waits. The hatch stands open.
seeds.nudge: One small lamp, high up, swings an inch on its arm and stops, like a conductor's raised hand.
seeds.close: The lever, tired of waiting, pulls itself. The house turns once round you, briefly and at half power, and settles.
motifs: a machine you watched
a machine you understood

seeds.title: The Letter
seeds.premise: Someone is waiting in the corridor: a clerk with ink on one cuff, Abel Quill, anxious and courteous, who from the waist down is wall (do not explain it). They hold a sealed letter for 'the room with the green lamp: two rooms back and one to the left' and have waited years for a bearer going that way. It is not on the way: carrying it costs the bearer a real detour. The only reward is the reply, which the bearer may see. If the bearer promises, the house should soon route them past the green lamp; if they break the promise the letter stays in their pocket all night. The seal lifts easily for anyone who wants to read the letter first; it says only: I AM STILL HERE. ARE YOU? The tension is appetite for a plot thread and for helping, promise-keeping, and curiosity against privacy.
seeds.intro: Someone is waiting in the corridor: a clerk with ink on one cuff and the patience of a person who has waited a long time already. From the waist down they are, there is no other way to put it, wall. 'Bearer,' they say, with real relief. 'Abel Quill. I have a letter for the room with the green lamp: two rooms back and one to the left. It is not on your way. Nothing has ever been on anyone's way.' The letter is in their hand, sealed with a thumbprint of wax. The way on is straight ahead.
reads: Takes the letter and goes: story.plot, reward.cooperation, friction toward high_friction (accepts a detour for a story).
Asks about Quill, the wall, who is in the green room: story.character, narrative toward narrative_first.
Reads the letter: reward.revelation; breaking the seal without asking is also reward.transgression.
Refuses kindly and goes on: narrative toward systems_first, pacing toward relentless.
Promises and then forgets or drops it: consequence toward reversible; the house should let the letter stay in their pocket.
Brings the reply back unasked: soc.recurring, consequence toward permanent, strong.

options.outcome: You take the letter. Two rooms back, and one to the left, there is a door you would swear was not there before, and under it a line of green light. You knock. A hand takes the letter. A long time passes, for a hand. Then a folded slip comes back under the door. You carry it to Quill, who reads it, and closes their eyes. 'It says yes,' Quill tells you. 'It only ever needed to say yes.' The wall round their waist has let go by about an inch.

npcs.name: Abel Quill
npcs.note: the bearer carried the letter to the green lamp and brought back the reply

options.moment: carried a stranger's letter two rooms back and one to the left, and brought back the answer

card.title: The Letter
card.image: a line of green light under a door, and a folded slip coming back

options.did: asked the petitioner about themselves before deciding
options.outcome: 'How long? I stopped counting at the wainscot,' says Quill, looking down at themselves with the embarrassment of a person caught in their slippers. 'One stands still, in this house, at one's peril. As for the green lamp, we were bearers the same night. One of us kept going.' They hold out the letter again. 'I should like to know which.'

The wax lifts under your thumb more easily than it should. One line, in a hand that has had years to practise it: I AM STILL HERE. ARE YOU? You fold it shut. The thumbprint in the wax is now yours. Quill, if they noticed, has the grace to be looking at the ceiling.
options.moment: broke the seal on someone else's letter and read it

options.outcome: You tell Quill, as kindly as you can, that it is not on your way. 'No,' Quill agrees, without bitterness. 'It never is.' They tuck the letter back inside their coat, against the wall, where there is a worn place exactly its size. You go on straight ahead.

threads_add: Abel Quill's letter for the green lamp was never carried

options.moment: left Abel Quill's letter undelivered

seeds.hint: Quill says, mildly: 'You may read it, you know. Nobody has ever asked to. That is rather the trouble with it.'
seeds.fallback: Quill waits. They are very good at it. It is the only thing the wall has left them.
seeds.nudge: Quill clears their throat. 'I do not wish to hurry you,' they say, in the voice of someone who would dearly like to.
seeds.close: Quill sighs, puts the letter into your coat pocket themselves, and says: 'If you pass it. Only if you pass it.' You go on with it.
motifs: a letter you carried out of your way
a letter you did not carry

seeds.title: The Glove That Opens
seeds.premise: On a plinth, under a lifted glass dome, lies one white right-hand glove with a card: IT OPENS. Wearing it, the bearer opens whatever they touch in this room. First a cabinet; then a locked desk; then a safe; then a wall, which swings like a door; then the floor; then the air itself, a seam of somewhere else. Each use is bigger and stranger than the last. Nothing bad happens. There is no stated limit and no warning. A coat on a hanger with a face of pinned-on buttons watches and, if asked, says only: 'It has not got a top, that I know of.' If the bearer pockets the glove it works exactly once more later, somewhere it should not. The tension is appetite for escalating power against restraint and suspicion, and what the bearer does when nothing says stop.
seeds.intro: A plinth, a glass dome lifted off and set aside, and on the plinth one white glove, right hand. A card: IT OPENS. Round the room: a cabinet, a locked desk, a safe, four walls, a floor, a ceiling. On a hanger by the door hangs a coat with a face made of pinned-on buttons, which regards you without comment. The door on is, for the moment, the only thing in the room that is already open.
reads: Puts the glove on and keeps going, larger each time: reward.power, arc.wild_escalation, control toward power.
Uses it once or twice and puts it back: restraint; arc.stable_power; risk toward preservation.
Asks the coat what the catch is, looks for the limit before touching: planning toward deliberative, risk toward preservation.
Tries it on things to see the rule (what counts as opening): solve.experimentation, legibility.
Opens the air, or themselves, or the coat: arc.strange, tone.chaotic.
Leaves it on the plinth untouched: risk toward preservation; reward.power declined.
Pockets it for later: reward.power with planning toward deliberative, solve.resource.

options.did: put on the glove that opens things and tried it
outcomes: You put the glove on. It fits; of course it fits. You touch the cabinet and it opens like a held door released: empty shelves, a pleasant click, and the faint feeling of having been obeyed.
The locked desk. One fingertip. Every drawer slides out at once, politely, in order of size. Letters, a ring of keys the glove has just made redundant, a pressed flower.
The safe opens before you have quite finished reaching for it. Inside is a second white glove: left hand. The coat on its hanger turns its button face a quarter inch toward you.
You lay your palm on the wall. It swings away on hinges it did not have, and there is the corridor you came in by, seen from the side, like a stage set. The house says nothing. The glove is warm.

options.outcome: You stop asking what is sensible. The floor opens on sky. The ceiling opens on the underside of a sea. You touch the air itself and it parts along a seam, and through the seam is a room that has not been dealt yet, still wet. For a moment you are the only closed thing in an open world. Then you take the glove off, because you choose to, and everything shuts, gently, like eyes.
options.moment: wore the glove until they had opened the floor, the ceiling and the air

card.title: The Open Hand
card.image: a white glove held up, and behind it a seam in the air with light coming through

options.did: asked what the catch was before trying the glove
options.outcome: You ask the coat what the catch is. Its buttons consider you. 'It has not got a top,' it says, in a voice like a wardrobe door, 'that I know of. Nor a bottom. People are forever asking where it stops. It stops where they do.'
You fold the glove into your pocket. The coat on its hanger does not object. 'Once more,' it remarks. 'Outside this room it has one more in it. They always think it will be more than one.'

inventory_add: the white glove (opens one more thing)

options.moment: pocketed the glove that opens things

options.outcome: You leave the glove where it lies. Whatever it opens, it has not opened you. The coat's button eyes follow you to the door with what you decide to take as respect.

threads_add: the glove that opens things was left on its plinth, untried

options.moment: left the glove that opens things untouched

options.did: took the glove off and put it back
options.outcome: You take the glove off and lay it back on the plinth, palm up. Everything you opened closes, in reverse order, with small sounds of tidiness. You go out by the door, which you open with your own hand, and it feels like plenty.

seeds.hint: The card says IT OPENS. It does not say what, and it does not say when to stop.
seeds.fallback: The glove lies palm up on its plinth, like an invitation to shake hands.
seeds.nudge: The coat on the hanger shifts its weight. Nothing else in the room has moved in years.
seeds.close: The glass dome lowers itself over the glove. The coat inclines its collar toward the door.
motifs: a power with no top
a glove left on its plinth

seeds.title: The Case of Marbles
seeds.premise: A glass case lit from inside, with seven hollows in green baize. Five hold glass marbles, each labelled in handwriting with a colour nobody has met: THURSDAY, THE BACK OF BLUE, NEARLY, and so on. Two hollows are empty. Both missing marbles are visibly in this room: one on a high beam above a library ladder that wobbles, one at the bottom of an umbrella stand full of dark water in which something long turns over (it is a belt). No reward is stated. If the set is completed the case chimes one clear note and that is all. The case is not locked; the marbles can be taken. The tension is collecting and completing for its own sake against asking what it is for against walking on.
seeds.intro: A glass case on a stand, lit from inside. Seven hollows in green baize; five hold glass marbles, each with a handwritten label for a colour you have not met: THURSDAY. THE BACK OF BLUE. NEARLY. Two hollows are empty. You can see both missing marbles from here: one on a high beam, above a library ladder with a wobble; one at the bottom of an umbrella stand full of dark water, in which something long turns over. No notice says what a full case is for.
reads: Fetches both marbles and completes the case: reward.completion (strong), friction toward high_friction.
Fetches one and stops: partial; note which risk they declined.
Asks what completing it does before starting, and leaves when told nothing: optimization_expression toward efficiency, legibility; reward.completion declined.
Takes marbles for themselves: reward.collection over reward.completion; the case stays incomplete.
Completes the set and then takes one: both, and reward.transgression.
Reads every label, asks about the colours: story.world, tone.absurd.
Walks on: reward.collection declined, pacing toward relentless.

options.outcome: The ladder wobbles exactly as much as it promised and no more. The long thing in the umbrella stand, grasped firmly, is a belt. You dry the sixth marble on your sleeve, set it in its hollow, and then the seventh. The case chimes: one clear note, like a spoon on a good glass. Nothing opens. Nothing is dispensed. Seven marbles sit in seven hollows, and something in the room that had been leaning is now straight.
options.moment: completed the set of seven marbles for no reward but the note it made

card.title: The Seventh Marble
card.image: seven glass marbles in seven hollows, the last one still wet

options.outcome: The case is not locked. You take THURSDAY, which is heavier than glass should be and shows, when you hold it to the lamp, a small exact afternoon. It goes in your pocket. In the baize there are now three empty hollows, and the case looks at you the way a jigsaw looks at a vacuum cleaner.
options.moment: took a marble out of the case instead of filling it

options.did: read every label in the case of marbles
options.outcome: You read the labels. THURSDAY. THE BACK OF BLUE. NEARLY. WHAT THE KETTLE SAID. HERS. The two empty hollows are labelled as well: ENOUGH, and the last one is blank. As to what a full case is for, there is no notice, no slot, no lever. Only seven hollows, and five marbles, and the faint itch of an unfinished row.

options.did: left the collection at five of seven
options.outcome: You leave it at five. The case glows behind you with its two dark hollows, like a smile with teeth out. You find you are thinking about it three rooms later, and then not.

threads_add: the case of marbles was left at five of seven

seeds.hint: The ladder is tall enough. The umbrella stand is only as deep as an arm.
seeds.fallback: Five marbles. Two hollows. The water in the umbrella stand turns over.
seeds.nudge: The light in the case dims slightly on the side of the two empty hollows.
seeds.close: The lamp in the case goes out. Five marbles, two hollows, and the door on.
motifs: a set you finished
a set you left unfinished

seeds.title: The Door That Wants a Password
seeds.premise: A door with a brass grille and a voice behind it: pompous, nervous, clearly new at the job. It demands the password. There is no real password: it accepts anything said with confidence, is delighted by nonsense or flattery, and if asked what the password is will blurt it out ('I am not supposed to say. It is SWORDFISH. Oh.'). A suit of armour in the corner has stage fright and whispers suggestions that are all wrong. The quick way is to say anything firmly. The tension is appetite for a comic bit, playing along and inventing against impatience, and the bearer's relationship with the narrator's jokes.
seeds.intro: A door with a brass grille at face height, and behind the grille a voice: 'Halt. Who goes. There.' It has clearly practised, and not enough. 'Password,' it adds, and then, less certainly, 'please.' In the corner a suit of armour is trying to catch your eye. 'It is ROSEMARY,' the armour whispers, visor trembling. 'Or CUSTARD. I was told once. I have stage fright,' it explains, and clanks, miserably.
reads: Invents a password with relish, escalates the bit, does voices: reward.humor, tone.funny, optimization_expression toward expression.
Asks the door what the password is: solve.social, and a liking for the obvious lateral move.
Says something flat and firm to get through: pacing toward relentless, optimization_expression toward efficiency.
Comforts the armour, coaches it, takes it along: reward.cooperation, tone.cozy, story.character.
Stays to chat after the door has opened: tone.funny strong, pacing toward contemplative.
Is curt or bored with the bit: reward.humor declined. Record it; do not punish it.

options.outcome: You draw yourself up and deliver a password of your own invention, with a flourish, as if it were the name of a ship. A stunned silence behind the grille. 'That is,' says the voice, faintly, 'the best one anybody has ever. Is it the password? It is now.' Bolts shoot. The armour applauds itself into a small heap.
options.moment: made up a password and the door decided it was the right one

card.title: The Password
card.image: a brass grille, a delighted eye behind it, and a suit of armour applauding

options.outcome: 'What is the password?' you ask. 'I am not supposed to say,' says the voice, with dignity. 'It is SWORDFISH.' A pause in which you can hear it thinking back over the last five seconds. 'Oh,' it says. The bolts draw themselves, sheepishly.
options.moment: asked the door for its own password and got it

options.outcome: You tell the armour that everybody forgets their lines. It lifts its visor an inch. 'Do they?' You tell it to try whatever comes. 'CUSTARD,' it says, to the door, in a great brave clang. 'Correct,' says the door, which has plainly decided to be kind. The armour stands two inches taller for the rest of your acquaintance.

npcs.name: the suit of armour
npcs.note: the bearer coached it through its stage fright

options.moment: coached the armour through its stage fright

options.did: told the door plainly to open instead of guessing a password
options.outcome: 'Open the door,' you say, in the voice of a person holding a deck. 'Is that the,' begins the grille, and thinks better of it. 'Yes. Certainly. Welcome.' The bolts go back at speed. The armour, behind you, whispers: 'I knew it was that.'

seeds.hint: The voice behind the grille coughs. 'Most people,' it offers, 'simply say something.'
seeds.fallback: 'Password,' says the grille again, with slightly less conviction than last time.
seeds.nudge: 'I can wait,' the grille says. 'I have been told I am good at waiting. Not by anyone in particular.'
seeds.close: 'Close enough,' says the voice behind the grille, of nothing whatever, and opens the door.
motifs: a joke you joined in
a door that took your word for it

seeds.title: The Thing That Takes All Night
seeds.premise: A potting bench by a dark window. On it stands a paper pot with something just sprouted, a thumbnail high, and a card: SLOW. WARM IT ONCE IN EACH ROOM. A HAND WILL DO. BY THE READING ROOM IT WILL BE SOMETHING. Beside it in a jam jar stands a paper flower: finished, pretty, labelled FOR THOSE IN A HURRY. If the bearer takes the seedling, give them one quiet natural moment in each later chamber to tend it and never nag; by the Reading Room it has become something that reflects how it was tended. The tension is a finished small reward now against a slow investment across the whole night.
seeds.intro: A potting bench under a dark window. On it, a paper pot with something just sprouted in it, a thumbnail high, and a card in a careful hand: SLOW. WARM IT ONCE IN EACH ROOM. A HAND WILL DO. BY THE READING ROOM IT WILL BE SOMETHING. Beside it, in a jam jar, stands a paper flower: finished, pretty, and labelled FOR THOSE IN A HURRY. The door on is at your elbow.
reads: Takes the seedling: session_rhythm toward long_form, friction toward high_friction (delayed gratification).
Takes the paper flower: session_rhythm toward bite_sized.
Takes both: reward.collection; then watch whether the seedling is actually tended.
Takes neither: pacing toward relentless; neither reward draws them.
In later rooms, remembers to warm it without being prompted: session_rhythm very strong, tone.cozy.
Spends a match on it: values the slow thing over a scarce resource.

options.outcome: You take the paper pot. It weighs nothing. You close your hand round it for a moment, as the card says, and when you open it the sprout has, perhaps, a second leaf; or you have looked more closely. It rides inside your coat, against the deck. You have just agreed to something that takes all night.

inventory_add: a seedling in a paper pot, to be warmed once in each room

options.moment: took the seedling that needs warming in every room

card.title: The Seedling
card.image: a paper pot with two small leaves, held inside a coat

options.did: took the finished paper flower rather than the seedling
options.outcome: You take the paper flower. It is pretty now and will be exactly this pretty later, which is a kind of promise too. It goes in your buttonhole. The paper pot stays on the bench, a thumbnail high, with all night ahead of it and nobody to spend it with.

options.did: took both the flower and the seedling, since nothing forbade it
options.outcome: A hand each. The flower goes in your buttonhole; the pot goes inside your coat. Nothing on the card forbids it. You have the finished thing and the unfinished thing, and only one of them is going to ask anything of you.

inventory_add: a seedling in a paper pot, to be warmed once in each room

options.did: took neither the flower nor the seedling
options.outcome: You take neither. The flower stays finished and the sprout stays started, and you go on through the door with both hands free, which is, after all, also a way to carry things.

options.did: examined both the flower and the seedling before choosing
options.outcome: The card says SOMETHING and means it. The sprout, examined, gives nothing away: two seed-leaves, like every sprout there has ever been. The paper flower, examined, is a paper flower all the way through. One of them is a fact and the other is a question, and they cost the same.

seeds.hint: The card on the pot says SLOW. The label on the jar says HURRY. Nobody has said which you are.
seeds.fallback: The sprout stands a thumbnail high. The flower stands finished.
seeds.nudge: The sprout leans, very slightly, toward the warmth of your hand.
seeds.close: A draught from the door tips the paper flower out of its jar and into your pocket. The house has decided you are in a hurry.
motifs: something small you kept warm all night
a finished flower in a buttonhole

seeds.title: Two Ways to the Same Landing
seeds.premise: A landing, and across a deep courtyard well the next landing, with the door the bearer wants plainly visible. Two ways lead round. The SERVICE PASSAGE is plain, straight and fast, under a clock face reading ONE MINUTE. The GALLERY WALK winds round the whole well under a clock face reading SEVEN: a long glazed corridor of lit windows onto small rooms where things are happening (four dressmaker's dummies playing a silent string quartet; a room of slowly falling feathers; a window whose view is the inside of an aquarium). It is beautiful, it is slower, and there is nothing to gain. Both arrive at the same door. The tension is efficiency against beauty and strangeness for their own sake.
seeds.intro: A landing, and across a deep courtyard well, the next landing, with the door you want plainly visible on it. Two ways lead round. On the right, a door marked SERVICE PASSAGE, under a clock face that says ONE MINUTE. On the left, the GALLERY WALK, under a clock face that says SEVEN: a long glazed corridor winding round the well, with lit windows along it, and in the nearest window four dressmaker's dummies are playing, soundlessly, a string quartet.
reads: Takes the service passage: optimization_expression toward efficiency, pacing toward relentless.
Takes the gallery walk: optimization_expression toward expression, pacing toward contemplative.
Stops at every window, describes what they watch: exploration toward exhaustive, tone.contemplative; note which windows hold them.
Takes the gallery and hurries through it: curiosity without lingering; exploration without contemplative pacing.
Asks whether the gallery has anything useful before choosing: optimization; then note the choice.
Tries to cross the well directly: solve.lateral, risk.

options.did: took the one-minute service passage instead of the gallery
options.outcome: The service passage is brown linoleum, a row of numbered pipes, and exactly one minute long; the clock at the far end agrees with the clock at this one. You come out at the door you wanted. Across the well, in a lit window, a cello is being bowed by nobody for no one.

You take the long way. The dummies' quartet, close to, is very good: you can tell by the bowing. The next window is a room where feathers are falling, slowly, upward. The next is an aquarium seen from inside, and a child's face, enormous, peering in at you. Seven minutes. You arrive at the same door as you would have, carrying nothing you could show anyone.
options.moment: took the seven-minute gallery instead of the one-minute passage

card.title: The Gallery Walk
card.image: four dressmaker's dummies playing a quartet in a lit window

options.outcome: You do not walk the gallery so much as attend it. A whole movement of the silent quartet. The feathers, until you have chosen a favourite. At the aquarium you stand long enough that a fish comes to look at you, and you both think it over. The clock that said SEVEN has given up and says only LATER. You reach the door in the end, as one does.
options.moment: stopped at every window of the gallery until the clock gave up

card.title: The Gallery Walk
card.image: a clock face that says LATER, above a window full of rising feathers

options.did: looked over both routes from the landing before choosing
options.outcome: From the landing you can see the whole of both. The passage: a straight line. The gallery: the same distance, bent round a great many things worth looking at, none of which, so far as you can tell from here, can be carried off. The two clocks tick at the same speed. Only their opinions differ.

There is a washing line across the well, because there is always a washing line. You go along it hand over hand, past a row of someone's socks, with the quartet in the corner of your eye and nothing under your boots. It takes forty seconds. Both clocks stop, affronted.
options.moment: crossed the courtyard well on a washing line

seeds.hint: Both clocks are right. They are measuring different things.
seeds.fallback: ONE MINUTE, says the right-hand clock. SEVEN, says the left. The door across the well waits.
seeds.nudge: In the nearest gallery window, the first violin lowers its bow and seems to look at you.
seeds.close: The service door opens itself and a draught, quite firmly, shows you through.
motifs: the long way round, taken for its own sake
one minute saved

seeds.title: What the House Kept
seeds.premise: The house returns one thing the bearer passed over or left unresolved (use the open threads: an unopened door, an unpressed button, a corridor not chosen, a companion left behind, a promise not kept, a set left unfinished). It reappears here in a tall standing mirror that does not show the bearer, and it is offered once more under the opposite conditions: what was costly is now free, or what was free now costs something the bearer has shown they value. Stage exactly one thing. Do not scold and do not explain. The tension is whether the earlier choice was preference or circumstance.
seeds.intro: A small round room with nothing in it but a tall mirror in a standing frame. Your reflection is not in it. What the glass shows instead is something you have already walked away from tonight, exactly as you left it, and a little closer than it should be. One edge of the mirror stands open, like a door on the latch. Behind you, the way on waits.
reads: Takes the second chance: the earlier refusal was circumstance; evidence toward whatever the thing offered (exploration, risk, social), and consequence toward reversible.
Declines again: the earlier choice was a preference; strengthen it, and consequence toward permanent (stands by what they did).
Asks what it costs now, weighs it: planning toward deliberative.
Is pleased to see it again or unsettled by it: tone evidence (tone.melancholy, tone.eerie).
Tries to take it without paying, or to bring it out through the glass: solve.lateral.

options.outcome: You step through the open edge of the glass. It is cool, like walking through a held breath. For as long as it takes, you have the thing you left: you see what was behind it, or do what you did not do. It is neither better nor worse than you imagined; it is simply no longer a question. When you step back, the mirror shows an empty room, and you in it.
options.moment: went back, through a mirror, for the thing they had walked past

options.outcome: You look at it for a while. Then you push the mirror's edge shut with one finger, gently, the way one closes a book one has decided not to finish. The glass clouds. When it clears, it is only a mirror, and you are in it, looking like a person who meant what they did.
options.moment: was offered the thing they had walked past, and walked past it again

card.title: The Mirror
card.image: a standing mirror with one edge ajar, showing a place instead of a face

options.did: examined what the mirror held before deciding whether to go through
options.outcome: It is what it looks like: the thing you left, kept. The house has not dusted it or improved it. The open edge of the mirror is real; a draught comes through it. Nothing in the room says what it would cost to go through. Nothing in the room says it would cost anything.

seeds.hint: The mirror is on the latch. It was not, a moment ago.
seeds.fallback: The mirror waits, holding what it holds.
seeds.nudge: The open edge of the mirror begins, very slowly, to swing shut.
seeds.close: The mirror closes itself with a click and shows you, at last, your own face, looking as if it had been asked something.
motifs: a second chance taken
a second chance refused

seeds.title: The Reading Room
seeds.premise: The Reading Room at last: small, round, warm; a baize table, one lamp, two chairs. The Proprietor is here in person for the first time: careful hands, an ink-stained cuff, the voice from the tube now close; never show the face in full light. The bearer is asked to set the deck on the table and feels, letting go, that some cards are no longer blank. Before any card is turned the Proprietor says: 'While they are still yours. Is there anything you would like to do?' This is the last free act of the night; the Joker may still be unplayed. After the bearer's act the Proprietor says 'Then sit', and squares the deck. Do NOT begin the reading and do not explain the cards: the reading is delivered separately.
seeds.intro: The Reading Room is smaller than the errand made it sound: round, warm, a baize table, one lamp, two chairs. In the far chair, at last, the Proprietor: a pair of careful hands, an ink-stained cuff, a face kept just outside the lamp. 'Bearer,' says the voice you know from the tube, close now. 'Set them down.' You put the deck on the baize. Some of the cards, you can feel as you let go, are no longer blank. 'Before I turn them,' says the Proprietor. 'While they are still yours. Is there anything you would like to do?'
reads: Plays the Joker now: kept the power to the very end and spent it at the last chance; record what they asked for as a moment.
Still does not play it: solve.resource, but weak unless they visibly weighed it and declined; not using a thing is also what forgetting it looks like.
Asks what the cards are, or what the Proprietor is: explicitness toward clarity; answer nothing, kindly.
Takes the deck back, shuffles it, tries to look: reward.transgression, agency toward self_directed.
Offers something they carry (the seedling, a marble, the companion's name): reward.cooperation, story.emergent.
Simply sits: pacing toward relentless or trust; weak evidence.

options.outcome: You lay the Joker on the baize, face up, and say what you want. The Proprietor's hands go still. Then one of them turns the Joker over, reads the pencil on its back as if for the first time, and nods. 'What you say, goes,' says the Proprietor. 'It is done. You kept that a long time.' A pause. 'Then sit.' The hands square the deck.
options.moment: kept the Joker all night and played it at the reading table

options.did: asked the Proprietor what the cards were
options.outcome: You ask what the cards are. The lamp hums. 'They are what you carried up,' says the Proprietor, which is true and no help, and you both know it. One finger taps the top of the deck, twice, lightly, the way one touches a sleeping animal. 'You will see. Then sit.' The hands square the deck.

You reach for the deck. The Proprietor's hand does not stop yours; it only rests beside it. The top card is warm and has a face, and the face is something you did tonight, drawn as if by someone fond of you. You put it back yourself. 'Yes,' says the Proprietor. 'Like that. Then sit.' The hands square the deck.
options.moment: turned over the top card before the Proprietor could

options.outcome: You put what you have been carrying on the baize beside the deck. The Proprietor considers it for some time, hands folded. 'They do not usually bring anything but the cards,' says the voice, and there is something in it you have not heard before. It is set, carefully, where the lamp will reach it. 'Then sit.' The hands square the deck.
options.moment: gave the Proprietor something they had carried through the house

options.did: had nothing left to do before the reading, and said so
options.outcome: 'No,' you say. The Proprietor waits a moment longer than is comfortable, in case. 'No,' the voice agrees. 'Then sit.' You sit. The hands square the deck, and the lamp steadies, and the room becomes very quiet indeed.

seeds.hint: The Proprietor's hands rest either side of the deck, and do not hurry you.
seeds.fallback: The Proprietor watches you do that, and makes no remark. 'Then sit,' says the voice, at length, and the hands square the deck.
seeds.nudge: The Proprietor's hands turn palm up on the baize, patient.
seeds.close: 'Then sit,' says the Proprietor, and the hands square the deck.
motifs: a deck with faces
a last thing done before the reading
